slides.heading: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
slides.body_md: Part 1 — compounds with a C–O bond: what they are, how they are named and how they are made.

rows: Hand sanitiser, fuel blended with petrol

visual.alt: Table of familiar alcohols, phenols and ethers and where they are met

slides.narration: Namaste! Sanitiser on your hands, ethanol blended into petrol, the phenol in old carbolic soap and the glycerol in cosmetics all contain a carbon–oxygen single bond. When an O–H group is attached to a saturated carbon we have an alcohol; when it is attached directly to a benzene ring, a phenol; and when oxygen joins two carbon groups, an ether. In this part we learn to classify, name and make them.

slides.heading: Classification
slides.body_md: Alcohols are **mono-, di- or trihydric** by the number of –OH groups, and **1°, 2° or 3°** by the carbon carrying –OH. **Allylic** and **benzylic** alcohols have –OH on an sp³ carbon next to C=C or a ring. **Phenols** have –OH on an aromatic carbon. **Ethers** are **symmetrical** (R–O–R) or **unsymmetrical** (R–O–R′).

visual.alt: Table classifying alcohols, a phenol and an ether with examples and structures

slides.narration: Alcohols are sorted in two ways. By the number of hydroxyl groups they are monohydric, dihydric like ethane-1,2-diol used in antifreeze, or trihydric like glycerol. By the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group they are primary, secondary or tertiary, just like haloalkanes. A phenol has the hydroxyl group directly on a benzene ring, which changes its chemistry a lot. Ethers have oxygen bonded to two carbon groups.

slides.heading: Naming
slides.body_md: Alcohols: replace the final **-e** of the alkane by **-ol**, with a locant (propan-2-ol). Phenols: named as derivatives of phenol (2-methylphenol). Ethers: **alkoxyalkanes**, the larger group being the parent (methoxyethane).

visual.alt: Table of common and IUPAC names of alcohols, phenols and ethers

slides.narration: For alcohols, take the name of the longest chain containing the hydroxyl carbon, drop the final e and add ol, with a number for the position: propan-two-ol. Phenols keep the name phenol, with substituents numbered from the hydroxyl carbon: two-methylphenol. Ethers are named as alkoxy alkanes: the smaller group becomes the alkoxy prefix, so ethyl methyl ether is methoxyethane, and anisole is methoxybenzene.

slides.heading: Structure: bond angles at oxygen
slides.body_md: Oxygen is sp³ hybridised with two lone pairs. In methanol the C–O–H angle (108.9°) is slightly less than tetrahedral (lone-pair repulsion); in ethers the C–O–C angle (about 111.7°) is larger because the bulky alkyl groups repel. In phenol the C–O bond (136 pm) is shorter than in methanol (142 pm) — partial double-bond character.

slides.narration: The oxygen atom in alcohols and ethers is sp three hybridised, with two lone pairs. In methanol, the lone pairs squeeze the carbon, oxygen, hydrogen angle slightly below the tetrahedral value, to about one hundred and nine degrees. In ethers, two bulky alkyl groups push each other apart, opening the angle to about one hundred and twelve degrees. In phenol, the oxygen lone pair is shared with the ring, so the carbon–oxygen bond is a little shorter.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming and classifying
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name and classify (a) $\ce{CH3CH2C(CH3)2OH}$, (b) $\ce{CH2=CHCH2OH}$, (c) $\ce{C6H5CH(OH)CH3}$, (d) $\ce{(CH3)2CHOCH3}$.

**(a)** 2-Methylbutan-2-ol — tertiary alcohol.

**(b)** Prop-2-en-1-ol — allylic, primary alcohol.

**(c)** 1-Phenylethan-1-ol — benzylic, secondary alcohol.

**(d)** 2-Methoxypropane — unsymmetrical ether.

nodes.label: Find the longest chain with the C–OH

visual.alt: Flow for naming and classifying an alcohol

slides.narration: In the first example, the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group has three carbon neighbours, so it is tertiary, and the name is two-methylbutan-two-ol. The second has the hydroxyl next to a double bond: an allylic alcohol, named prop-two-en-one-ol. The third is next to a benzene ring, a benzylic secondary alcohol. The last is an ether: the smaller methyl group becomes methoxy and the parent is propane.

slides.heading: Alcohols from alkenes
slides.body_md: **Acid-catalysed hydration** adds water by Markovnikov’s rule (via a carbocation). **Hydroboration–oxidation** (B₂H₆, then H₂O₂/OH⁻) adds water **anti-Markovnikov**, giving primary alcohols from terminal alkenes.

visual.alt: Table of alkene hydration products by acid-catalysed hydration and hydroboration–oxidation

slides.narration: Alkenes can be turned into alcohols by adding water across the double bond. With an acid catalyst, the reaction goes through a carbocation, and the hydroxyl group ends up on the more substituted carbon, following Markovnikov’s rule: propene gives propan-two-ol. Hydroboration followed by oxidation does the opposite, putting the hydroxyl group on the end carbon: propene gives propan-one-ol.

slides.heading: Alcohols from carbonyl compounds
slides.body_md: **Reduction:** aldehydes give 1° alcohols, ketones give 2° alcohols (H₂ with Pd/Pt/Ni, or NaBH₄, LiAlH₄). Acids and esters are reduced to 1° alcohols by LiAlH₄. **Grignard reagents** add to carbonyl compounds; hydrolysis gives alcohols: methanal → 1°, other aldehydes → 2°, ketones → 3°.

visual.alt: Table showing that Grignard reagents with methanal, other aldehydes and ketones give primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols

slides.narration: Carbonyl compounds are the other big source of alcohols. Reducing an aldehyde gives a primary alcohol; reducing a ketone gives a secondary alcohol. Grignard reagents are even more useful, because they also make a new carbon–carbon bond. With methanal they give primary alcohols, with other aldehydes secondary alcohols, and with ketones tertiary alcohols, once the magnesium compound is hydrolysed with dilute acid.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a Grignard synthesis
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Which carbonyl compound and Grignard reagent would you use to make (a) propan-1-ol, (b) butan-2-ol, (c) 2-methylpropan-2-ol?

**(a)** $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr}$ + methanal (HCHO) → $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$ (1°).

**(b)** $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr}$ + ethanal ($\ce{CH3CHO}$) → $\ce{CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3}$ (2°).

**(c)** $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ + propanone ($\ce{CH3COCH3}$) → $\ce{(CH3)3COH}$ (3°).

Each adduct is hydrolysed with dilute acid.

nodes.label: Break one C–C bond to the carbinol carbon

visual.alt: Flow for planning a Grignard synthesis by breaking a bond to the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group

slides.narration: Work backwards from the target. Look at the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group and imagine cutting one of its carbon–carbon bonds. The piece you cut off becomes the alkyl group of the Grignard reagent; the rest, with the hydroxyl turned into a carbonyl group, is the carbonyl compound. For two-methylpropan-two-ol, cutting off a methyl group leaves propanone, so methylmagnesium bromide and propanone are needed.

slides.heading: Preparation of phenol
slides.body_md: Phenol is made from **haloarenes** (Dow process), **benzenesulfonic acid** (fusion with NaOH), **diazonium salts** (warming with water) and, commercially, from **cumene**.

visual.alt: Table of four ways to prepare phenol with conditions

slides.narration: Phenol cannot be made by simply adding water to benzene, so other routes are used. Chlorobenzene can be forced to react with sodium hydroxide at high temperature and pressure. Sodium benzenesulfonate can be fused with sodium hydroxide. A diazonium salt gives phenol simply on warming with water. In each case the phenoxide salt is acidified to release phenol.

slides.heading: The cumene process
slides.body_md: Most phenol is made from **cumene** (isopropylbenzene). Air oxidises it to **cumene hydroperoxide**, which dilute acid splits into **phenol and propanone** — two valuable products.

visual.alt: Flow of the cumene process from benzene and propene through cumene and its hydroperoxide to phenol and propanone

slides.narration: Industry makes most of its phenol by the cumene process. Benzene and propene combine to give cumene. Air oxidises cumene to a hydroperoxide, which breaks apart in dilute acid into phenol and propanone. The process is economical because both products are useful: propanone, also called acetone, is an important solvent.

slides.heading: Worked example: phenol from a diazonium salt
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** How would you convert aniline into phenol? Give the conditions.

**Step 1.** Diazotise: aniline + $\ce{NaNO2}$ + HCl at 273–278 K gives benzenediazonium chloride.

**Step 2.** Warm the solution: $\ce{C6H5N2Cl + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl}$.

**Step 3.** Nitrogen bubbles off; phenol is obtained (steam distillation separates it).

visual.alt: Table of the two steps and conditions for converting aniline into phenol

slides.narration: This is a common two-step conversion. First, aniline is diazotised with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid in an ice bath, because diazonium salts decompose if they get warm. Then the solution is deliberately warmed, so the diazonium group is replaced by a hydroxyl group from water, and nitrogen gas bubbles out.

slides.heading: Physical properties
slides.body_md: Alcohols and phenols form **hydrogen bonds**, so they boil much higher than alkanes, haloalkanes or ethers of similar mass. Lower alcohols are **miscible with water** (they hydrogen-bond to it); solubility falls as the hydrocarbon part grows. Boiling point rises with chain length and falls with branching.

visual.alt: Table comparing boiling points of ethanol, methoxymethane and propane of similar molar mass

slides.narration: Ethanol, methoxymethane and propane all have molar masses near forty five, yet ethanol boils at three hundred and fifty one kelvin, about a hundred degrees higher than the other two. The difference is hydrogen bonding between ethanol molecules. Ethers have no O–H hydrogen, so they cannot hydrogen-bond to each other. Small alcohols dissolve in water because they hydrogen-bond with water molecules.

slides.heading: Hydrogen bonding in alcohols
slides.body_md: The H of one O–H group is attracted to a lone pair on the O of a neighbouring molecule.

slides.narration: Here you can see why alcohols are sticky at the molecular level. The hydrogen of each hydroxyl group is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of the next molecule, forming hydrogen bonds. To boil the alcohol, these must be broken, which needs extra energy. Alcohol molecules can also form hydrogen bonds with water, which is why ethanol and water mix in all proportions.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Alcohols: 1°, 2°, 3°, allylic, benzylic; mono-, di-, trihydric. Phenols: –OH on an aryl carbon. Ethers: R–O–R′.
Names: alkanol (propan-2-ol); substituted phenols; alkoxyalkanes (methoxyethane).
O is sp³; C–O–H 108.9°, C–O–C 111.7°; C–O in phenol shorter (partial double bond).
Alcohols from alkenes (H⁺ hydration: Markovnikov; hydroboration: anti-Markovnikov), carbonyl reduction and Grignard reagents.
Phenol from chlorobenzene, benzenesulfonate, diazonium salts and cumene.
Hydrogen bonding gives high boiling points and water solubility.

visual.alt: Summary table of Grignard reactions giving primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. We classify alcohols by the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group, name them as alkanols, and name ethers as alkoxy alkanes. Oxygen is sp three hybridised. Alcohols come from alkenes, from reduction of carbonyl compounds and from Grignard reagents; phenol comes from chlorobenzene, sulfonates, diazonium salts and cumene. Hydrogen bonding explains their high boiling points and solubility in water.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Grignard: methanal → 1°, other aldehydes → 2°, ketones → 3° alcohols; always add "then H₃O⁺".
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov; acid hydration is Markovnikov.
Cumene process: name both products (phenol and propanone).
Diazotisation is done at 273–278 K; warming gives phenol.
Compare boiling points using hydrogen bonding, not just molar mass.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Learn the Grignard pattern by heart: methanal, aldehyde, ketone give primary, secondary, tertiary alcohols. Remember which hydration method puts the hydroxyl group where. In the cumene process, name both products. Keep diazotisation cold. And when comparing boiling points, always discuss hydrogen bonding.

slides.heading: Reactions of alcohols, phenols and ethers
slides.body_md: Part 2 — acidity, reactions of the O–H and C–O bonds, the activated ring of phenol, and ethers.

visual.alt: Flow of reaction types: breaking the O–H bond gives acidity and esterification; breaking the C–O bond gives reactions with HX and dehydration; phenol also reacts at the ring

slides.narration: Alcohols and phenols react in two main ways. Some reactions break the oxygen–hydrogen bond, as when they act as acids or form esters. Others break the carbon–oxygen bond, as when they react with hydrogen halides or lose water. Phenol also has a very reactive benzene ring. In this part we compare their acidity, study their reactions, look at two important alcohols and finish with ethers.

slides.heading: Acidity of alcohols and phenols
slides.body_md: Alcohols react with active metals to give alkoxides and hydrogen, but are **weaker acids than water**. **Phenol** is much more acidic: it dissolves in NaOH, because the **phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance**. Neither reacts with $\ce{NaHCO3}$.

visual.alt: Table of pKa values of ethanol, water, phenol and substituted phenols

slides.narration: Ethanol reacts with sodium, releasing hydrogen, so it is acidic, but only very weakly: even water is a stronger acid. Phenol is about a million times more acidic than ethanol and dissolves in sodium hydroxide solution. Look at the table: a smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Electron-withdrawing nitro groups make phenol more acidic; an electron-releasing methyl group makes it slightly less acidic.

slides.heading: Why phenol is more acidic
slides.body_md: In phenoxide the negative charge is **delocalised** over oxygen and the ortho and para carbons; in ethoxide it stays on oxygen, and the alkyl group even **pushes electrons** towards it (+I). Electron-withdrawing groups at **ortho/para** (–NO₂) spread the charge further and increase acidity.

slides.narration: Why is phenol so much more acidic? When phenol loses a proton, the negative charge on the phenoxide ion spreads into the ring, onto the ortho and para carbons, as these resonance structures show. Spreading charge stabilises an ion. In the ethoxide ion, the charge is stuck on oxygen, and the ethyl group pushes even more electron density onto it. A nitro group at ortho or para spreads the charge still further.

slides.heading: Worked example: ranking acidity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange in increasing acidity: ethanol, phenol, 4-nitrophenol, 4-methylphenol, water.

**Step 1.** Ethanol < water (alkyl +I effect destabilises ethoxide).

**Step 2.** Phenols are far more acidic than water (resonance in phenoxide).

**Step 3.** Among phenols: –CH₃ (+I) lowers acidity, –NO₂ at para (–R, –I) raises it.

**Answer.** Ethanol < water < 4-methylphenol < phenol < 4-nitrophenol.

visual.alt: Table ranking ethanol, water, 4-methylphenol, phenol and 4-nitrophenol by pKa with the effect in each

slides.narration: Rank acidity by thinking about the stability of the ion left after the proton leaves. Ethoxide is destabilised by the ethyl group, so ethanol is the weakest acid, just below water. All phenoxides are stabilised by the ring. A methyl group adds electron density and slightly destabilises the ion, while a nitro group at the para position withdraws electrons and stabilises it most.

slides.heading: Reactions of alcohols: esterification, HX and dehydration
slides.body_md: **Esterification** (O–H breaks): with carboxylic acids (H⁺ catalyst, reversible), acid chlorides or anhydrides. **With HX** (C–O breaks): reactivity 3° > 2° > 1° (Lucas test). **Dehydration** with conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄: ethanol gives ethene at 443 K (ether at 413 K); ease 3° > 2° > 1° (carbocation stability).

headers: Lucas test (conc. HCl + ZnCl₂, room temperature)

visual.alt: Table of Lucas test observations for tertiary, secondary and primary alcohols

slides.narration: With carboxylic acids and a little sulfuric acid, alcohols form sweet-smelling esters; the reaction is reversible. With hydrogen halides, the carbon–oxygen bond breaks. Tertiary alcohols react fastest because they form stable carbocations, which is the basis of the Lucas test: tertiary alcohols turn the reagent cloudy at once, secondary in a few minutes, primary not at all at room temperature. Hot concentrated sulfuric acid removes water to form alkenes.

slides.heading: Oxidation of alcohols
slides.body_md: Oxidation removes H from O–H and from the C bearing –OH. **1° alcohols** → aldehydes (PCC, or Cu at 573 K) → carboxylic acids (acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇). **2° alcohols** → ketones. **3° alcohols** resist oxidation; over hot Cu they dehydrate to alkenes.

visual.alt: Table of oxidation products of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols with dichromate and over hot copper

slides.narration: Oxidation tells primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols apart. A primary alcohol loses hydrogen to become an aldehyde, which strong oxidants carry on to a carboxylic acid; pyridinium chlorochromate stops at the aldehyde. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so it resists oxidation; over hot copper it loses water to give an alkene instead.

slides.narration: Quick check. Recall which compounds dissolve in sodium hydroxide, and what each class of alcohol gives on oxidation.

slides.heading: Electrophilic substitution in phenol
slides.body_md: The –OH group strongly **activates** the ring and directs to **ortho and para** positions. Phenol reacts with **bromine water** at room temperature to give a white precipitate of **2,4,6-tribromophenol**; in CS₂ at low temperature, mono-bromophenols form. Dilute HNO₃ gives o- and p-nitrophenol; concentrated HNO₃ gives **picric acid**.

visual.alt: Table of electrophilic substitution reactions of phenol with bromine and nitric acid

slides.narration: The hydroxyl group pushes electron density into the ring, especially at ortho and para positions, so phenol reacts with electrophiles far faster than benzene. Bromine water instantly gives a white precipitate of tribromophenol, a useful test. In a non-polar solvent at low temperature, only one bromine goes in. Dilute nitric acid gives ortho and para nitrophenols, which can be separated by steam distillation because the ortho isomer has intramolecular hydrogen bonding.

slides.heading: Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions
slides.body_md: **Kolbe’s reaction:** sodium phenoxide + CO₂ (about 400 K, 4–7 atm), then acid → **salicylic acid** (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). **Reimer–Tiemann reaction:** phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH, then acid → **salicylaldehyde** (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde).

visual.alt: Table of Kolbe, Reimer–Tiemann, zinc dust and oxidation reactions of phenol

slides.narration: Two named reactions put a new carbon group onto the ring of phenol, at the ortho position. In Kolbe’s reaction, sodium phenoxide is heated with carbon dioxide under pressure, giving salicylic acid, the starting material for aspirin. In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, phenol is heated with chloroform and sodium hydroxide, giving salicylaldehyde. Phenol is also reduced to benzene by hot zinc dust.

slides.heading: Worked example: distinguishing tests
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give a chemical test to distinguish (a) ethanol and phenol; (b) propan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

**(a)** Add **bromine water**: phenol decolourises it and gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; ethanol does not. (Or neutral FeCl₃: violet colour with phenol.)

**(b)** **Lucas reagent** at room temperature: 2-methylpropan-2-ol turns cloudy at once; propan-1-ol stays clear.

visual.alt: Table of tests distinguishing ethanol from phenol and a primary from a tertiary alcohol

slides.narration: Distinguishing tests must give a clear, visible difference. Phenol decolourises bromine water and forms a white precipitate, and it gives a violet colour with neutral iron three chloride; ethanol does neither. To tell a primary alcohol from a tertiary one, use Lucas reagent: the tertiary alcohol turns cloudy at once, while the primary alcohol shows no change at room temperature.

slides.heading: Methanol and ethanol
slides.body_md: **Methanol** is made from synthesis gas, $\ce{CO + 2H2}$ over ZnO–Cr₂O₃ at high temperature and pressure; it is very poisonous (blindness, death). **Ethanol** is made by **fermentation** of sugars (molasses, starch) using yeast enzymes; denatured alcohol has methanol and a dye added so it cannot be drunk.

rows: Solvent for paints and varnishes; making methanal
Solvent, sanitisers, beverages, biofuel blended with petrol

visual.alt: Table of uses and hazards of methanol and ethanol

slides.narration: Methanol, sometimes called wood spirit, is made from carbon monoxide and hydrogen over a catalyst. It is a useful solvent but highly poisonous: even small amounts can cause blindness. Ethanol is made by fermenting sugars from molasses or starch with yeast, whose enzymes invertase and zymase break sucrose into glucose and then glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. India blends ethanol into petrol to reduce oil imports.

slides.heading: Ethers: preparation
slides.body_md: **Williamson synthesis:** an alkoxide or phenoxide reacts with a **primary** alkyl halide by SN2. With tertiary halides elimination dominates, so the tertiary group must be on the alkoxide. **Dehydration** of primary alcohols (conc. H₂SO₄, 413 K) gives symmetrical ethers.

visual.alt: Table of correct and incorrect Williamson choices for tert-butyl methyl ether and anisole

slides.narration: The best laboratory route to ethers is Williamson’s synthesis: an alkoxide ion attacks an alkyl halide in an S N two reaction. The alkyl halide should be primary. If you try a tertiary halide, the strongly basic alkoxide pulls off a hydrogen instead and you get an alkene. So to make tert-butyl methyl ether, use sodium tert-butoxide with bromomethane, not the other way round.

slides.heading: Ethers: reactions
slides.body_md: Ethers are fairly unreactive. **HI** cleaves the C–O bond: with mixed alkyl ethers, the halide goes to the **smaller** (methyl) group (SN2), or to the **tertiary** group (SN1). Aryl alkyl ethers give **phenol + alkyl iodide**. The –OR group of anisole activates the ring for **o/p electrophilic substitution**.

visual.alt: Table of reactions of anisole: cleavage with HI, bromination, nitration and Friedel–Crafts acylation

slides.narration: Ethers are good solvents precisely because they are unreactive, but hot hydrogen iodide cleaves them. In methoxyethane, iodide attacks the less hindered methyl carbon, giving iodomethane and ethanol. In anisole, the phenyl–oxygen bond has partial double-bond character, so it is the methyl–oxygen bond that breaks: phenol and iodomethane form. The methoxy group also activates the ring, so anisole undergoes ortho and para substitution.

slides.heading: Worked example: products of ether cleavage
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Predict the products with excess-free HI (one equivalent): (a) 1-methoxypropane; (b) 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane; (c) ethoxybenzene.

**(a)** $\ce{CH3I}$ + propan-1-ol (SN2 at the less hindered methyl).

**(b)** $\ce{(CH3)3CI}$ + methanol (SN1: stable tertiary carbocation).

**(c)** Phenol + iodoethane (aryl–O bond does not break).

visual.alt: Table of ether cleavage products by mechanism

slides.narration: Decide which carbon the iodide attacks. With a methyl and a primary group, the mechanism is S N two, so iodide attacks the smaller methyl carbon. With a tertiary group, the protonated ether breaks to give a stable tertiary carbocation, which picks up iodide, so the iodide ends up on the tertiary carbon. With an aryl ether, the aryl–oxygen bond never breaks, so phenol is always one product.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Acidity: alcohols < water < phenols; phenoxide resonance-stabilised; –NO₂ (o/p) increases, –CH₃ decreases acidity.
Alcohols: esterification; HX (3° > 2° > 1°, Lucas test); dehydration to alkene (443 K) or ether (413 K); oxidation 1° → aldehyde → acid, 2° → ketone, 3° resists.
Phenol: bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol; nitration; Kolbe → salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann → salicylaldehyde.
Methanol from CO + 2H₂ (toxic); ethanol by fermentation (invertase, zymase).
Ethers: Williamson (alkoxide + 1° halide); HI cleavage; anisole o/p-substitution.

visual.alt: Summary table of tests for phenol and tertiary alcohols

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Phenols are much more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance. Alcohols form esters, react with hydrogen halides, lose water and are oxidised according to their class. Phenol’s ring is strongly activated, giving tribromophenol, nitrophenols, salicylic acid and salicylaldehyde. Methanol and ethanol are important industrially, and ethers are made by Williamson’s synthesis and cleaved by hydrogen iodide.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: For acidity questions, compare the stability of the anions (resonance, +I, −I, −R).
Name the reagent and the observation in distinguishing tests.
Williamson: alkoxide + primary halide; never a tertiary halide.
HI cleavage of anisole gives phenol + CH₃I, not iodobenzene.
Write "then H₃O⁺" for Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some final tips. In acidity questions, always talk about the stability of the ion formed. In tests, give both reagent and observation. In Williamson syntheses, the halide must be primary. Remember that anisole and hydrogen iodide give phenol, not iodobenzene. And note that phenol is too weak an acid to react with sodium hydrogencarbonate, which is how phenols are told apart from carboxylic acids.

sections.heading: 1. Classification, nomenclature and structure
sections.body_md:
**Alcohols:** mono-, di-, trihydric; 1°, 2°, 3° by the carbon bearing –OH; allylic and benzylic alcohols; vinylic/aryl –OH are enols/phenols. **Phenols:** –OH on an aromatic carbon (phenol, cresols, catechol, resorcinol, quinol). **Ethers:** R–O–R (symmetrical) or R–O–R′ (unsymmetrical).

**IUPAC:** alkan-n-ol (propan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, propane-1,2,3-triol); substituted phenols (2-methylphenol, benzene-1,2-diol); ethers as alkoxyalkanes (methoxyethane, methoxybenzene = anisole, 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane).

**Structure:** O is sp³ with two lone pairs. C–O–H in methanol 108.9°; C–O–C in methoxymethane about 111.7° (bulky groups repel). In phenol the C–O bond (136 pm) is shorter than in methanol (142 pm): partial double-bond character from resonance and the sp² carbon.

key_terms.definition_md: An alcohol whose –OH carbon is bonded to one other carbon.
A compound with –OH directly attached to an aromatic ring carbon.
An ether whose two groups on oxygen are different.

sections.heading: 2. Preparation of alcohols and phenols
sections.body_md:
**Alcohols:**
- Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes (Markovnikov): propene → propan-2-ol.
- Hydroboration–oxidation (B₂H₆; H₂O₂/OH⁻): anti-Markovnikov, propene → propan-1-ol.
- Reduction: aldehydes → 1°, ketones → 2° (H₂/Pd, Ni; NaBH₄; LiAlH₄); acids and esters → 1° (LiAlH₄).
- Grignard reagents + carbonyl compounds, then hydrolysis: HCHO → 1°, RCHO → 2°, R₂CO → 3°.

**Phenol:**
- From chlorobenzene: NaOH at 623 K, 300 atm, then acid.
- From benzenesulfonic acid: fuse the sodium salt with NaOH, then acid.
- From diazonium salts: warm with water, $\ce{C6H5N2Cl + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl}$.
- **Cumene process:** $\ce{C6H5CH(CH3)2 + O2 -> C6H5C(CH3)2OOH}$; $\ce{C6H5C(CH3)2OOH ->[H+] C6H5OH + CH3COCH3}$ (phenol + propanone).

sections.heading: 3. Physical and chemical properties of alcohols and phenols
sections.body_md:
**Physical:** hydrogen bonding gives high boiling points (ethanol 351 K vs methoxymethane 248 K and propane 231 K); lower alcohols are miscible with water; bp rises with chain length and falls with branching.

**Acidity:** alcohols < water < phenol (pKa: ethanol 15.9, water 15.7, phenol 10.0). Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised; electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂ at o/p) increase acidity (4-nitrophenol 7.1, picric acid 0.5); electron-releasing groups (–CH₃) decrease it. Alcohols and phenols react with Na; phenol also with NaOH; neither with NaHCO₃.

**Alcohols:** esterification $\ce{CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=>[H+] CH3COOC2H5 + H2O}$; with HX (3° > 2° > 1°; Lucas test); with PX₃, SOCl₂; dehydration (conc. H₂SO₄: ethanol → ethene at 443 K, → ethoxyethane at 413 K; ease 3° > 2° > 1°); oxidation 1° → aldehyde (PCC or Cu, 573 K) → acid (KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇), 2° → ketone, 3° resist (alkene over hot Cu).

**Phenol:** –OH activates the ring (o/p): bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt); Br₂ in CS₂ at 273 K → mono-bromophenols; dilute HNO₃ → o- and p-nitrophenol (o-isomer steam-volatile, intramolecular H-bond); conc. HNO₃ → picric acid. **Kolbe:** sodium phenoxide + CO₂ → salicylic acid. **Reimer–Tiemann:** CHCl₃ + NaOH → salicylaldehyde. Zn dust → benzene; Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ → benzoquinone. Neutral FeCl₃ gives a violet colour.

Carboxylation of sodium phenoxide with CO₂ to give salicylic acid.
Formylation of phenol with CHCl₃ and NaOH to give salicylaldehyde.

sections.heading: 4. Commercially important alcohols
sections.body_md:
**Methanol (wood spirit):** $\ce{CO + 2H2 ->[ZnO/Cr2O3] CH3OH}$ (573–673 K, 200–300 atm). Solvent for paints and varnishes; used to make methanal. Highly poisonous: small quantities cause blindness, larger ones death.

**Ethanol:** fermentation of molasses or starch. $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[invertase] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$; $\ce{C6H12O6 ->[zymase] 2C2H5OH + 2CO2}$. Solvent, sanitisers, beverages, fuel blended with petrol. Industrial alcohol is **denatured** (methanol and a dye such as pyridine added) to make it unfit to drink.

key_terms.definition_md: Ethanol made unfit to drink by adding methanol and other substances.
Slow breakdown of sugars by enzymes of yeast to ethanol and carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: 5. Ethers
sections.body_md:
**Preparation:** Williamson synthesis — alkoxide/phenoxide + **primary** alkyl halide (SN2): $\ce{C2H5ONa + CH3I -> C2H5OCH3 + NaI}$. With 3° halides, elimination occurs, so the bulky group must be on the alkoxide. Dehydration of 1° alcohols at 413 K gives symmetrical ethers.

**Physical:** bp close to alkanes of similar mass (no H-bonding between molecules); solubility in water similar to alcohols of similar size (they H-bond to water).

**Reactions:** cleavage by HI (or HBr): methyl alkyl ethers → CH₃I + alcohol (SN2 at methyl); tertiary alkyl ethers → tertiary halide + methanol (SN1); aryl alkyl ethers → phenol + alkyl halide ($\ce{C6H5OCH3 + HI -> C6H5OH + CH3I}$). Anisole: –OCH₃ activates the ring, o/p-directing — bromination in ethanoic acid gives mainly 4-bromoanisole; nitration and Friedel–Crafts reactions give mainly para products.

key_terms.definition_md: Preparation of ethers by reaction of an alkoxide or phenoxide with a primary alkyl halide.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using a tertiary alkyl halide in a Williamson synthesis (elimination occurs).
- Writing iodobenzene as a product of anisole + HI (phenol + CH₃I form).
- Saying phenol reacts with NaHCO₃ (it is weaker than carbonic acid).
- Forgetting "then H₃O⁺/acidify" in Grignard, Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions.
- Saying tertiary alcohols oxidise to ketones.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: product, reagent, name or order.
- Conversions (2–3 marks): reagent and condition per step (½–1) + correct product.
- Acidity explanations: compare the stability of the conjugate bases (resonance, +I/−I/−R) (1–2 marks).
- Tests: reagent (½–1) + observation for each compound (½–1).

questions.stem_md: $\ce{C6H5CH(OH)CH3}$ is best described as a:
questions.solution_md: The –OH carbon is joined to two carbons (the ring carbon and CH₃), so it is secondary, and it is next to the benzene ring, so benzylic — option (a). It is not a phenol (c), because –OH is not on a ring carbon.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH(OH)CH3}$ is:
questions.solution_md: Longest chain with the –OH carbon: five carbons. Number from the end giving –OH the lower locant: OH at C2, methyl at C4 — option (b). (a) gives –OH the higher number.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of $\ce{C6H5OCH2CH3}$ is:
questions.solution_md: Ethers are named as alkoxy derivatives of the larger parent: the benzene ring with an ethoxy group — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The C–O bond in phenol (136 pm) is shorter than the C–O bond in methanol (142 pm) because:

options.text_md: phenol forms stronger hydrogen bonds than methanol
oxygen in phenol is sp hybridised
phenol has a lower molar mass than methanol
the oxygen lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring and the ring carbon is sp² hybridised

questions.solution_md: Resonance gives the C–O bond partial double-bond character, and an sp² carbon forms a shorter bond than an sp³ carbon — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Prop-2-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH, is a vinylic alcohol.
questions.solution_md: False. The –OH is on an sp³ carbon next to the C=C, so it is an allylic alcohol. A vinylic –OH would be on a carbon of the double bond itself.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of glycerol, HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH, is propane-1,2,3-___.
questions.solution_md: Three –OH groups: propane-1,2,3-**triol**.

questions.stem_md: Match each common name with its IUPAC name.
questions.solution_md: Anisole = methoxybenzene; o-cresol = 2-methylphenol; catechol = benzene-1,2-diol; tert-butyl alcohol = 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

questions.stem_md: Write the structures of (a) 3-methylbutan-2-ol and (b) 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane, and classify each compound.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH(CH3)CH3}$: the –OH carbon is bonded to two carbons, so it is a **secondary alcohol**. (b) $\ce{(CH3)3COCH3}$: oxygen joins a methyl and a tert-butyl group, so it is an **unsymmetrical ether**.

questions.solution_md: Draw the parent chain, add substituents, classify.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of reagents, followed by dilute acid, gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol?
questions.solution_md: A tertiary alcohol needs a ketone. Ethyl from the Grignard reagent + (CH₃)₂C=O gives (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃ — option (d). (a) gives butan-2-ol (2°); (b) gives propan-1-ol (1°).

questions.stem_md: Propene is treated with diborane and the product is then oxidised with alkaline hydrogen peroxide. The alcohol formed is:
questions.solution_md: Hydroboration–oxidation adds water anti-Markovnikov: –OH goes to the terminal carbon — option (b). Acid-catalysed hydration would give propan-2-ol (a).

questions.stem_md: Reduction of butan-2-one with sodium borohydride gives:
questions.solution_md: Reduction of a ketone gives a secondary alcohol with the same carbon skeleton: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the cumene process, cumene hydroperoxide is treated with dilute acid. The products are:
questions.solution_md: $\ce{C6H5C(CH3)2OOH ->[H+] C6H5OH + CH3COCH3}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Benzenediazonium chloride solution is warmed. What happens?

options.text_md: Chlorobenzene is formed without any gas.
Nitrogen gas is evolved and phenol is formed.
Benzene is formed and chlorine is evolved.

questions.solution_md: $\ce{C6H5N2Cl + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl}$ — option (b). Chlorobenzene (a) needs CuCl (Sandmeyer).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The cumene process is economically attractive for making phenol.

**Reason (R):** It produces propanone, another useful chemical, along with phenol.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the valuable by-product propanone is the main reason the process is economical — option (a).

questions.stem_md: How would you obtain phenol from (a) chlorobenzene, (b) aniline and (c) cumene? Give reagents and conditions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Heat with NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm to give sodium phenoxide, then acidify: $\ce{C6H5Cl + 2NaOH -> C6H5ONa + NaCl + H2O}$.

(b) Diazotise with $\ce{NaNO2}$/HCl at 273–278 K, then warm with water: $\ce{C6H5N2Cl + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl}$.

(c) Oxidise with air to cumene hydroperoxide, then treat with dilute acid: phenol + propanone.

questions.solution_md: Dow process; diazonium hydrolysis; cumene process.

questions.stem_md: Using a Grignard reagent and a suitable carbonyl compound each time, show how to make (a) propan-1-ol, (b) propan-2-ol, (c) 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr}$ + HCHO, then $\ce{H3O+}$ → $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$.

(b) $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ + $\ce{CH3CHO}$, then $\ce{H3O+}$ → $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH3}$.

(c) $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ + $\ce{CH3COCH3}$, then $\ce{H3O+}$ → $\ce{(CH3)3COH}$.

questions.solution_md: Methanal → 1°, aldehyde → 2°, ketone → 3°.

questions.stem_md: Ethanol (M = 46) boils at 351 K, while methoxymethane (M = 46) boils at 248 K. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: ethanol has a larger molar mass
ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another; methoxymethane molecules cannot
methoxymethane is more polar than ethanol

questions.solution_md: Both have the same molar mass; only ethanol has an O–H group for intermolecular hydrogen bonding — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A colourless compound dissolves in aqueous NaOH but not in aqueous NaHCO₃, and gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃. It is most likely:
questions.solution_md: Phenol is acidic enough to react with NaOH but too weak to release CO₂ from NaHCO₃ (benzoic acid would, c), and phenols give a violet colour with FeCl₃ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Phenol is shaken with excess bromine water at room temperature. The product is:
questions.solution_md: The –OH group strongly activates the ortho and para positions: $\ce{C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr}$ — option (b). Monobromination (a) needs Br₂ in CS₂ at low temperature.

questions.stem_md: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.solution_md: The para nitro group withdraws electrons (−R, −I) and stabilises the phenoxide ion (pKa 7.1) — option (b). Methyl (+I) weakens phenol; ethanol is far weaker.

questions.stem_md: Three alcohols, P, Q and R, are mixed with Lucas reagent at room temperature. P turns cloudy at once, Q after about five minutes, and R stays clear. P, Q and R could be:
questions.solution_md: Rate with Lucas reagent: 3° (instant) > 2° (minutes) > 1° (no turbidity at room temperature) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Vapours of three alcohols are passed over heated copper at 573 K. Which alcohol gives an alkene rather than a carbonyl compound?
questions.solution_md: 1° and 2° alcohols are dehydrogenated to aldehydes and ketones; a 3° alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon and is dehydrated to 2-methylpropene instead — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Ethanol is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid at 413 K, with ethanol in excess. The main organic product is:
questions.solution_md: At 413 K intermolecular dehydration gives the ether: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O — option (a). At 443 K, ethene (b) is the main product.

questions.stem_md: Sodium phenoxide is heated with carbon dioxide under pressure and the product is acidified. The compound obtained is used to make:
questions.solution_md: Kolbe’s reaction gives salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid), which is acetylated to aspirin — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Phenol is warmed with chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide, and the mixture is then acidified. The main product is:
questions.solution_md: Reimer–Tiemann reaction: a –CHO group is introduced mainly at the ortho position — option (a). Salicylic acid (b) comes from Kolbe’s reaction.

questions.stem_md: A mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol is separated by steam distillation. Which distils over, and why?

options.text_md: 2-Nitrophenol, because intramolecular hydrogen bonding makes it more volatile
Both distil together, as they are isomers

questions.solution_md: In the ortho isomer the –OH hydrogen-bonds to the neighbouring –NO₂ within the molecule; the para isomer forms intermolecular H-bonds and is far less volatile — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol.

**Reason (R):** The phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its negative charge over the benzene ring.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the resonance stabilisation of phenoxide (absent in ethoxide) explains the greater acidity — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Tertiary alcohols are not easily oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate.

**Reason (R):** Tertiary alcohols react fastest with Lucas reagent.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Resistance to oxidation is due to the absence of a hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, not to their reactivity with Lucas reagent (which reflects carbocation stability) — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Propan-1-ol has a higher boiling point than butane, although their molar masses are similar.

**Reason (R):** Propan-1-ol is a non-polar molecule.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (hydrogen bonding in the alcohol). R is false: the O–H group makes propan-1-ol polar — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Phenol liberates carbon dioxide from sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.

**Reason (R):** Phenol is acidic enough to react with sodium hydroxide.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: phenol (pKa 10) is weaker than carbonic acid, so it does not liberate CO₂. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The pKa values of ethanol and phenol are 15.9 and 10.0. How many times larger is the acid dissociation constant of phenol? (Give the answer to 2 significant figures, in units of $10^{5}$.)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{K_\text{a}(\text{phenol})}{K_\text{a}(\text{ethanol})} = 10^{15.9 - 10.0} = 10^{5.9}$, and $10^{5.9} = 794328$. In units of $10^{5}$: $794328 \div 100000 = 7.94$, so the answer is about 7.9.

questions.stem_md: What volume of hydrogen, in litres at STP (22.4 L mol⁻¹), is released when $4.6\ \text{g}$ of ethanol reacts completely with sodium? ($M = 46\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $\ce{2C2H5OH + 2Na -> 2C2H5ONa + H2}$. Moles of ethanol $= \dfrac{4.6}{46} = 0.1$, so $0.05$ mol $\ce{H2}$; volume $= 0.05 \times 22.4 = 1.12$, so $1.12\ \text{L}$.

questions.stem_md: What mass of bromine, in grams, is needed to convert $0.94\ \text{g}$ of phenol completely into 2,4,6-tribromophenol? (Phenol $M = 94$; $\ce{Br2}$ $M = 160\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $\ce{C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr}$. Moles of phenol $= \dfrac{0.94}{94} = 0.01$; bromine $= 3 \times 0.01 = 0.03$ mol; mass $= 0.03 \times 160 = 4.8$, so $4.8\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: Explain why ethanol is a weaker acid than water.

answer.model_answer_md: In the ethoxide ion, the ethyl group releases electrons (+I effect) towards the negatively charged oxygen, intensifying the charge and destabilising the ion. Hydroxide has no such group. A less stable conjugate base means a weaker acid, so ethanol is weaker than water.

questions.solution_md: Compare the stability of ethoxide and hydroxide.

marking_scheme.step: +I effect of ethyl intensifies charge on O⁻
Less stable conjugate base, weaker acid

questions.stem_md: Give one chemical test each to distinguish (a) phenol from ethanol and (b) propan-2-ol from 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Add neutral FeCl₃ solution: phenol gives a violet colour, ethanol does not (or bromine water: white precipitate with phenol). (b) Add Lucas reagent at room temperature: 2-methylpropan-2-ol turns cloudy at once, propan-2-ol only after about five minutes.

questions.solution_md: Reagent and observation for each.

questions.stem_md: Explain why 2-methylpropan-2-ol is dehydrated by acid much more easily than ethanol.

answer.model_answer_md: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde and then, with acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇, to a carboxylic acid; PCC or hot copper stops at the aldehyde (e.g. CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO → CH₃COOH). A secondary alcohol gives a ketone (propan-2-ol → propanone). A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon and resists oxidation; over hot copper it dehydrates to an alkene. Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂) converts the alcohol to an insoluble chloroalkane, seen as turbidity: tertiary alcohols react at once, secondary in about five minutes, primary not at room temperature, because the rate depends on carbocation stability. Dehydration also proceeds through a carbocation, formed when protonated –OH leaves as water; tertiary carbocations are most stable, so tertiary alcohols dehydrate most easily.

answer.model_answer_md: Phenol loses H⁺ to give phenoxide, whose negative charge is delocalised over the ortho and para carbons; this resonance stabilisation makes phenol acidic (pKa 10). In ethoxide the charge stays on oxygen and is intensified by the +I ethyl group, so ethanol (pKa 15.9) is far weaker. In a carboxylate ion the charge is shared equally by two oxygen atoms, a better stabilisation, so carboxylic acids are stronger. A para nitro group withdraws electrons (−R, −I) and spreads the charge further, so 4-nitrophenol (pKa 7.1) is more acidic. Kolbe: sodium phenoxide + CO₂ at about 400 K and 4–7 atm, then acid, gives salicylic acid. Reimer–Tiemann: phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH, then acid, gives salicylaldehyde.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the Williamson synthesis, and explain why it fails with tertiary alkyl halides. Suggest how to make tert-butyl methyl ether.

(b) Write the products of the reaction of HI with methoxyethane and with anisole, and explain the difference.

(c) Explain why the methoxy group in anisole makes the ring more reactive and directs to ortho and para positions.

answer.model_answer_md: In the Williamson synthesis, an alkoxide or phenoxide ion attacks a primary alkyl halide by SN2, giving an ether: C₂H₅ONa + CH₃I → C₂H₅OCH₃ + NaI. With a tertiary halide, the strongly basic alkoxide removes a β-hydrogen instead and an alkene forms. So tert-butyl methyl ether is made from sodium tert-butoxide and bromomethane. With HI, methoxyethane gives iodomethane and ethanol, because iodide attacks the less hindered methyl carbon (SN2). Anisole gives phenol and iodomethane: the aryl C–O bond has partial double-bond character, and phenyl cannot undergo SN2, so only the methyl–O bond breaks. In anisole, a lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring (+R effect), increasing electron density, especially at the ortho and para positions, so electrophiles attack there faster than in benzene.

(b) Compare acid-catalysed hydration and hydroboration–oxidation of propene.

answer.model_answer_md: Benzene and propene give cumene (isopropylbenzene). Air oxidises cumene to cumene hydroperoxide, C₆H₅C(CH₃)₂OOH, which dilute acid splits into phenol and propanone. Its advantage is that propanone, a useful solvent, is produced at the same time. Acid-catalysed hydration of propene proceeds through the more stable secondary carbocation, so –OH adds to the middle carbon (Markovnikov) to give propan-2-ol; hydroboration with B₂H₆ followed by alkaline H₂O₂ places –OH on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov), giving propan-1-ol. Alcohol molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds between O–H groups, which must be broken on boiling; ethers cannot hydrogen-bond to one another, so they boil lower. Lower alcohols are miscible with water because their O–H groups form hydrogen bonds with water molecules and the hydrocarbon part is small.

questions.solution_md: Cumene steps and by-product; Markovnikov vs anti-Markovnikov; hydrogen bonding.
